summary:
Morocco criminalises same-sex conduct under Article 489 of the penal code, which punishes "indecent acts" between persons of the same sex with six months to three years of imprisonment. Outright International reports that the provision is applied with wide police discretion and that arrests are arbitrary; 170 people were charged with same-sex relations in 2018. Human Rights Watch recorded Article 489 in its April 2018 report "Audacity in Adversity" among the statutes used to punish same-sex conduct and gender expression across the wider region, and ILGA's State-Sponsored Homophobia survey lists Morocco among countries prohibiting same-sex activity between consenting adults.

Trans visitors face a further layer of exposure that the statute does not name. Cairo 52's country review finds no specific legal provisions governing transition, yet documents de facto criminalisation under Article 498, where morality charges follow gender-expression discrepancies and arrest produces involuntary outing. The Cairo 52 report "A Web of Violence" (January 2026), based on interviews with 17 trans and non-binary Moroccans, documents an interlocking system of legal, medical, social and economic hostility, and finds that Article 489 is weaponised to arrest trans people on the basis of gender expression.

There is no legal gender recognition pathway in Morocco. Cairo 52 records no gender-affirming healthcare framework, leading some Moroccans to self-medicate; a 2021 recognition process exists for intersex people only. The Grand Mufti opposes transition. Morocco once pioneered gender-affirming surgery for foreigners but now enforces a de facto prohibition for its own citizens.

Police conduct toward perceived trans people includes documented abuse. In November 2024 an Instagram model alleged that Moroccan police forced her to expose her genitals over suspicions that she was trans. In January 2019 El País reported that police in Marrakesh subjected a cross-dresser, Chafiq, to online humiliation after a minor traffic accident: he was handcuffed, filmed by bystanders and officers, his ID documents were photographed and posted online, and he subsequently sought asylum in Europe.

Public identification as LGBTIQ carries significant risk of violence and harassment, and authorities block LGBTIQ organisations. Human Rights Watch documented a 2020 campaign of online harassment of presumed gay and bisexual men; during that campaign some landlords ejected targeted tenants, and journalist Hicham Tahir reported receiving a hundred testimonies, with one person alleged to have died by suicide. A trans woman was violently beaten in Tangier in November 2022; three minors and an adult were arrested over the assault.

Morocco has no law against discrimination or harassment on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and no political party has enacted LGBTQ rights legislation. There is no legal recognition of same-sex couples. Police disproportionately target perceived LGBTQ people, and the names of arrested individuals are publicised before trial. In 2017 former Minister of Justice and Liberties Mustafa Ramid called homosexuals "trash" in an interview; local human rights associations petitioned Prime Minister Othmani to investigate what they termed his discriminatory and unconstitutional statements towards sexual minorities.

Enforcement has a documented record. In December 2007 a court in Ksar el-Kebir convicted six men under Article 489 after an online video of a private party, reported in the press as a "gay marriage", circulated; their lawyers said no evidence of prohibited conduct was presented, and the men were sentenced on 17 December 2007 to varying terms. Dozens then marched through the streets of Ksar el-Kebir calling for their punishment. In 2016 two girls in Marrakesh were arrested after a cousin photographed them kissing and their mother complained to police; both were acquitted in December 2016, provoking the #freethegirls outcry.

The government has banned books on homosexuality and requires schools to teach a curriculum that "emphasises ... the danger and depravity of unnatural acts". The 2018-19 Arab Barometer survey found 21% of Moroccan respondents said homosexuality is acceptable. The UN Human Rights Council adopted the SOGI resolution in September 2014, establishing an international human-rights scrutiny framework that applies to Morocco.
tangentialFactors:
Cairo 52's January 2026 report situates Morocco within a regional pattern of systemic erasure of transgender people, while noting that the country once pioneered gender-affirming surgery for foreigners, a historical distinction that no longer reflects domestic policy.

The April 2020 outing campaign extended beyond legal consequences into housing insecurity, with landlords ejecting targeted tenants, and sociologist Khalid Mouna framed the transgender influencer Sofia Talouni as seeking to isolate young Moroccan homosexuals by breaking up their family unit.

The Ksar el-Kebir convictions and the Marrakesh girls' case show that enforcement responds to private conduct captured on video or reported by family, not only to public visibility; the street marches after the 2007 verdict indicate community pressure for harsher punishment.

Public opinion is not uniform: 21% of respondents in the 2018-19 Arab Barometer survey said homosexuality is acceptable, though this figure measures attitudes to homosexuality rather than to gender identity specifically.
localsOnly:
Moroccan residents have no legal gender recognition pathway and no gender-affirming healthcare framework; a 2021 recognition process exists for intersex people only, and the absence of regulated care has led some to self-medicate.

Historical medical reference: 1950s publicity around the French entertainer Coccinelle helped establish Casablanca as a place where certain doctors were willing to perform sex change operations albeit in clandestine circumstances, indicating unregulated care rather than any documented public facility.

Residents face no statutory anti-discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and no political party has enacted LGBTQ rights legislation; the Grand Mufti opposes transition.

Names of arrested individuals are publicised before trial, and police disproportionately target perceived LGBTQ people, creating a permanent record risk for residents that does not apply in the same way to short-term visitors.

The government bans books on homosexuality and mandates a school curriculum that emphasises the danger and depravity of "unnatural acts", shaping the social environment residents navigate daily.
outOfScopeNotes:
No current trans-specific healthcare access, identity-document procedure, or shelter provision for trans visitors is recorded in the source inventory; the medical reference available is historical and describes clandestine, unregulated care rather than any documented public facility.

The scale of the April 2020 outing campaign rests on a single journalist's count of a hundred testimonies and one alleged suicide that is reported but not independently confirmed in the inventory.

The claim that Morocco enforces a de facto prohibition on gender-affirming surgery for its own citizens while permitting it for foreigners is asserted in the Cairo 52 report without a cited statutory or regulatory instrument in the inventory; the legal basis for the distinction is unresolved.

Whether Article 498 morality charges are routinely used against trans visitors specifically, as distinct from residents, is not separately quantified in the sources; the de facto criminalisation finding derives from Cairo 52's country review and interviews with Moroccan nationals.
